catalog_quote: 3. Stress. Stress is phonemically contrastive in Cayapa, as in hídyáʔ 'let's go!', hídeʔ 'go!', hídyiʔ 'go! (polite)', kídyáʔ 'let's make!'. Stress is so nearly predictable, however, (see following rules) that contrastive pairs are very hard to find and in our corpus pairs of the type just cited are the only ones available. Within the phonological word the following statements may be made concerning the placement of stress: (1) The first syllable is always stressed, e.g. pábába 'black'; (2) All heavy syllables (defined as CVC, CVV(C)--but not CVʔ) are stressed, e.g. ʔílyápáŋ 'shotgun'; (3) All nonfinal syllables not included in rules (1) and (2) or in the morphological observations below may be optionally stressed, e.g. kábúčúwa, kábučúwa 'rope'. Morphologically, some stresses are predictable in that stress always occurs on the first syllable of a stem, as in /mám+bípénu/ 'to bathe agai…

new_statements.quote: ACENTO. En cayapa las palabras presentan un acento principal y un acento secundario(I). El acento principal cae en la penúltima sílaba y el secundario en la antepenúltima. Esto ocurre con gran regularidad. Las excepciones a esta regla son muy raras y se deben a la entonación interrogativa. /hinu/ ['hi.nu] ... /iša/ ['i.ša] "frío" /makara/ [²ma.'ka.ra] "estrella" /mamuškenu/ [ma.²muš.'ke.nu] "deshacer" /nemi:pihpuka/ [ne.mi:.²pih.'pu.ka] "tobillo" /ka:nemiškelenu/ [ka:.ne.miš.²ke.'le.nu] "dedo meñique del pie". El acento puede cambiar de lugar debido a la entonación en palabras de dos sílabas: /muden/ [mu.'den] "¿quienes son?" /na:naⁱn/ [na:.'naⁱn] "¿donde?" (I. Representamos con el número 2 el acento secundario.)
new_statements.translation: STRESS. In Cayapa, words carry a primary stress and a secondary stress. The primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable and the secondary on the antepenultimate. This happens with great regularity. Exceptions to this rule are very rare and are due to interrogative intonation. [examples 'star' ma.'ka.ra, 'to undo' ma.muš.'ke.nu, 'ankle' ne.mi:.pih.'pu.ka, 'little toe' ka:.ne.miš.ke.'le.nu, each with secondary stress (raised 2) on the antepenult]. Stress may change place because of intonation in two-syllable words: mu.'den 'who are they?', na:.'naⁱn 'where?'. (Footnote I: We represent secondary stress with the numeral 2.)

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record (Lindskoog & Brend 1962: 39-40, re-read from the mirror) has stress marginally contrastive but 'so nearly predictable', with rule (1) 'The first syllable is always stressed', rule (2) all heavy syllables (CVC, CVV(C)) stressed, rule (3) other nonfinal syllables optionally stressed, plus stem-initial and lexically stressed suffixes (filed as weight-hedged, initial). Contreras Ponce states a regular, non-contrastive PENULTIMATE primary stress with secondary stress on the antepenult, the only exceptions being intonational (final stress in disyllabic question words), and his transcriptions throughout mark penult stress on words of three or more syllables irrespective of vowel…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is regular and non-contrastive: primary stress on the penultimate syllable, secondary stress on the antepenultimate; vowel length and closed syllables play no role in placement (long vowels and CVC syllables occur unstressed: [bi.nes.mu.'te.le], [ka.ne.miš.²ke.'le.nu], [luš.ka.'ta.ta]). The only displacement is to the final syllable of disyllabic words under interrogative intonation.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the antepenultimate syllable (immediately before the primary), marked with a raised '2' in his transcriptions: [²ma.'ka.ra], [ma.²muš.'ke.nu], [ne.mi.²pih.'pu.ka], [ka.ne.miš.²ke.'le.nu].
new_statements.exceptions: 'Las excepciones a esta regla son muy raras y se deben a la entonación interrogativa': in disyllabic question words stress moves to the final syllable ([mu.'den] '¿quienes son?', [na.'naⁱn] '¿donde?').
new_statements.identity_note: All four works and the catalog source describe the same language, Cha'palaa / Cayapa / Chachi [cbi], Esmeraldas province, NW Ecuador. Contreras Ponce 1982 describes the río Canandé dialect, with brief work with one río Cayapas speaker (thesis PDF p. 10); Lindskoog & Brend 1962 rest on Santiago Añapa of the Cayapas River (below the San Miguel confluence), data 1955-1961; Wiebe 1977 rests on eleven written narratives by bilingual Cayapa school teachers of the Cayapas river area; Julmi 2018 on fieldwork June-August 2018 (endangeredlanguages.ch report).

readall_conflicts: Real disagreement between primary sources. The catalog record rests on Lindskoog & Brend 1962 (SEIL I pp. 39-40, re-read from the mirror): stress marginally contrastive but 'so nearly predictable', rule (1) 'The first syllable is always stressed', rule (2) all heavy syllables (CVC, CVV(C)) stressed, rule (3) remaining nonfinal syllables optionally stressed, stem-initial stress and lexically stressed suffixes (filed weight-hedged, left edge). Contreras Ponce 1982 (ENAH thesis on the río Canandé dialect, open at the INAH repository, now in the mirror) states the opposite edge: primary stress regularly on the PENULTIMATE syllable, secondary on the antepenult, exceptions only intonational in disyllabic questions, and his transcriptions throughout the thesis mark penult stress on 3-to-6-syllable words regardless of vowel length or syllable closure ([bi.nes.mu.'te.le], [ka.ne.miš.²ke.'le.nu], [luš.ka.'ta.ta], [i.ka.'ka.nu]). The two agree only on disyllables (initial = penult). Wiebe 1977 (held, read) is silent; Abrahamson 1962 (only the 2-page text excerpt open; SIL file an automated-access block-walled, the Internet Archive check deferred) and Julmi 2018 (print-only, Zürich) remain unread and are the sources that could arbitrate, Julmi 2018 above all as a 127-page dedicated phonology. overall_reading is set to what the works opened in this item support (Contreras: fixed: penultimate syllable); the catalog's initial/weight-hedged record from Lindskoog & Brend stands against it an…
